name: Inflation & Purchasing Power
description: Inflation measures how quickly consumer prices rise, while purchasing power describes what income can buy. In Iran, understanding the relationship requires attention to exchange rates, fiscal and monetary conditions, household spending patterns, and the reporting period behind each statistic.

seo.title: Inflation and Purchasing Power in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s consumer price inflation, its relationship to household purchasing power, and the limits of available annual comparisons.

content.heading: Prices and the purchasing power of income
content.content:
Inflation describes the rate at which prices increase over a specified period. Consumer price inflation follows a basket of household purchases, rather than every transaction in an economy. Purchasing power connects those prices to income: when earnings rise more slowly than the cost of the basket, real income falls. A larger paycheck can therefore accompany a reduced ability to purchase goods and services. [s1]

Slower inflation does not reverse earlier price increases. It means prices are increasing less rapidly; a falling price level is a different phenomenon. Contracts also adjust at different speeds. Salaries and pensions may respond slowly, while some goods change price frequently, exposing households to a period in which expenditure rises before income catches up. [s1]

content.heading: Why inflation persists in Iran
content.content:
Research by H. Elif Ture and Ali Reza Khazaei examines Iran’s inflation using quarterly evidence spanning 2004–2021. Their model identifies currency depreciation, fiscal deficits, and sanctions, represented through oil exports, as influences operating over both shorter and longer horizons. Money growth emerges as a longer-term driver. These are model-based findings for the study period, rather than a mechanical explanation of every subsequent price movement. [s2]

The mechanisms interact. Reduced foreign exchange receipts can put pressure on the currency and increase the domestic cost of imports. Import restrictions can also constrain supply directly. Meanwhile, financing government deficits through the domestic banking system can expand money creation. The paper consequently treats external restrictions and domestic policy as connected influences, rather than competing explanations that can be cleanly separated. [s2]

The authors also caution that administered prices can suppress measured increases temporarily while creating other costs. Their policy discussion is an analytical assessment, not evidence that a particular reform was implemented successfully. [s2]

content.heading: Reading the recent annual figures
content.content:
The World Bank’s October 2026 outlook reports elevated annual inflation throughout the short series below. The final historical period is explicitly an estimate. These figures preserve the publication’s reporting labels; they should not be relabeled as Gregorian calendar-year observations. [s3]

Source choice matters. The Bank’s Spring 2024 monitor reported a different inflation figure for 2023/24. The series here uses the later outlook consistently instead of combining publication vintages. Reconciliation with the underlying consumer price index remains necessary before publication. [s3][s4]

content.heading: What the headline cannot establish
content.content:
A national consumer price index represents a weighted basket, not the precise experience of every household. Comparing purchasing power also requires evidence about earnings, transfers, and actual spending needs. The inflation series alone cannot establish how much a particular family’s living standard changed. [s1]

The useful conclusion is therefore conditional: sustained price increases create pressure on incomes that fail to keep pace. Measuring the size and distribution of that pressure requires a matched income-and-price analysis, which is not available in this draft. [s1]

name: Unemployment
description: Iran’s unemployment rate measures joblessness among people participating in the labor force, rather than among all adults. Participation, employment, working hours, and differences between population groups are essential to interpreting the headline.

seo.title: Unemployment and Labor Force Participation in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Read Iran’s unemployment figures alongside labor force participation, employment, and differences between women, men, and younger workers.

content.heading: Who counts as unemployed?
content.content:
In international labor statistics, unemployment is a specific status. It generally combines being without work, being available to work, and actively seeking employment. The labor force includes employed and unemployed people; people outside it are excluded from the unemployment-rate denominator. Someone who wants a job but has stopped searching may therefore disappear from the headline measure without finding employment. [s1]

This distinction is central to reading Iran’s figures. An unemployment rate describes difficulty finding work among labor force participants. A participation rate asks how much of the working-age population is economically active. An employment-to-population ratio asks how much is employed. Together, these measures reveal more than unemployment alone. [s1]

content.heading: Recovery with a participation problem
content.content:
The World Bank’s Spring 2024 monitor reported unemployment of 8.1 percent in 2023/24 alongside labor force participation of 41.3 percent. Employment had recovered beyond its pre-pandemic level, but participation remained weak. The report attributed part of the decline in unemployment to discouraged people leaving the active labor force. [s2]

That combination changes the interpretation of an apparently favorable headline. More employment can represent a recovery while withdrawal from job search simultaneously reduces measured unemployment. Assessing the balance requires looking at employment and participation together, rather than assuming every fall in the unemployment rate represents a transition into work. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Different experiences within the national average
content.content:
For 2023/24, the monitor reported unemployment of 6.6 percent among men and 15 percent among women. It also identified higher unemployment among young people and university graduates. These are rates within their respective labor forces, not shares of all men, women, or graduates. [s2]

Sectoral change adds another dimension. The monitor described agricultural job losses associated with drought and water shortages, alongside employment expansion in industry and services. A national total can therefore conceal substantial changes in the location and type of work. [s2]

content.title: How the main labor market measures fit together
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Working-age population"] -->|"Participates in labor market"| B["Labor force"]
  A -->|"Outside labor force"| C["People outside the labor force"]
  B -->|"Has employment"| D["Employed people"]
  B -->|"Without work, available and seeking"| E["Unemployed people"]
  E -->|"Numerator divided by labor force"| F["Unemployment rate"]
```
content.summary: The unemployment rate uses the labor force as its denominator. People outside the labor force are excluded, even when they would like employment but do not meet the search or availability criteria.

content.heading: Reading a changing labor market
content.content:
The October 2026 World Bank outlook describes renewed labor market deterioration. Its recent quarterly discussion should not be appended to an annual unemployment series as though the periods were interchangeable. [s3]

Employment itself also leaves questions unanswered. Hours, earnings, informality, and working conditions help distinguish having work from having adequate work. Statistical comparisons additionally require consistent age thresholds, survey coverage, and definitions. For Iran, a reconciled annual series with those details is still needed; this draft therefore provides no trend chart. [s1]

name: Economic Growth
description: Economic growth measures changes in Iran’s real output, separating production from price increases. Its interpretation requires attention to oil and non-oil activity, population, employment, and revisions to national accounts.

seo.title: Economic Growth in Iran: Real Output and Its Limits | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s real GDP growth, the role of oil and external restrictions, and why output growth differs from household welfare.

content.heading: More production, rather than higher prices
content.content:
Gross domestic product, or GDP, measures final goods and services produced within an economy. Economic growth usually means the percentage change in real GDP: output measured after adjusting for price changes. Nominal output can rise because prices increase, even when production does not. Real growth is therefore the appropriate starting point for asking whether Iran’s economy is producing more. [s1]

Growth is a rate, not the size of the economy. A slower positive rate still indicates expansion; a negative rate indicates contraction. Nor does aggregate growth establish that average living standards improved. GDP does not describe how income is distributed, and it omits important dimensions of welfare, including environmental costs and unpaid household activity. [s1]

content.heading: A recovery that needs a longer perspective
content.content:
The World Bank’s publication overview describes Iran’s recovery after a prolonged period of negligible growth during 2011–2020. It identifies recovering consumption and more favorable oil-sector conditions among the forces behind the initial rebound following the pandemic shock. That history makes the starting point important: growth after a downturn does not by itself establish a return to an earlier development path. [s2]

The latest inspected outlook reports slower growth followed by an estimated contraction in the short annual series below. It also describes damage to productive infrastructure during conflict. These are the World Bank’s assessments; the estimated annual result remains subject to revision. [s3]

content.x_axis_label: Iranian reporting year, using the source’s Gregorian-span label
content.interpretation: The series moves from expansion to slower expansion and then an estimated contraction. The final observation is a source estimate, and the following forecast year is excluded.

content.heading: External restrictions and domestic transmission
content.content:
Research by Mehdi Raissi and M. Hashem Pesaran investigates sanctions using an indicator constructed from newspaper coverage. Its abstract reports effects on exchange rates, inflation, and output growth, with currency depreciation preceding higher inflation and weaker output. It also reports adverse effects on employment and participation. These findings provide an analytical explanation for links between external restrictions and domestic economic activity. [s4]

They do not establish that sanctions explain every fluctuation. An estimated relationship depends on the study’s identification strategy and period. Its counterfactual results should not be treated as observed production, and this page does not insert them into the annual dataset. The inspected abstract supports the broad findings summarized here, rather than a detailed assessment of the model. [s4]

content.heading: What to read alongside growth
content.content:
A useful assessment pairs real GDP with employment and distributional evidence. Positive growth may still be insufficient to create enough jobs, and changes in total output do not reveal who receives additional income. [s1]

For the annual comparison here, the reporting period and publication vintage are as important as the headline. A full historical account requires a longer, methodologically consistent series and reconciliation of revisions. Until that work is complete, the chart establishes the recent direction reported by one publication, rather than a complete account of Iran’s growth performance.
